articles.title: Regulating LAWS
articles.content: AT three o’clock on the morning of Saturday, Sept 5, 2026, Room III of the Palais des Nations in Geneva — the only room in the building with any sign of life — erupted in applause. The Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS), under the able leadership of its Dutch chair, had adopted — after three years of negotiations — a report containing elements of an instrument. On the final day, the delegations of the 128 high contracting parties to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) sat for 18 hours without a break. The report contains, for the first time, an agreed characterisation of LAWS. The subject has been under discussion in the CCW since 2014, and only now have states parties been able to say which systems fall under the label. The report also reaffirms that control and human judgement are needed to ensure compliance with international humanitarian law (IHL), that human beings must determine the measures necessary for that compliance. It sets out a non-exhaustive list of what those measures might be. Part of the applause that morning was relief, and part of the relief was that the text had survived at all. Over three years, a small number of militarily significant states, the very states developing and fielding these technologies, worked steadily to thin it out. ‘Human control’ became ‘judgement and control’, and then control that could be exercised indirectly. Predictability, reliability, and explainability, once framed as properties a system must possess, were dropped from the text altogether. A proposed requirement that a system must not alter its target parameters or its mission without human authorisation did not make it to the final agreement either. No new prohibitive norm survived. An honest reading of the text is that it gives a green light to the development and use of LAWS, provided certain measures are in place. Those measures are real, and they are better than nothing. But they focus on how the existing law applies to this category of systems. They fall well short of the joint appeal issued in October 2023 by the UN secretary-general and the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, who called on states to conclude by 2026 a legally binding instrument prohibiting autonomous weapon systems that operate without human control or that target human beings directly, and regulating all others. A handful of militarily significant states continue to resist any negotiation of a new legal instrument and are unlikely to accept one. Technology on the battlefield has always outpaced the human ability to govern it. Back in 2014, when the discussions first began, autonomous weapons were largely a matter of science fiction. They are not any more. Algorithmic decision-support systems have been used to generate targets at a speed no human can match. In various conflicts, loitering munitions and drones with autonomous terminal guidance have been used, precisely because they provide an advantage, are cheap, and keep working when the electronic warfare environment cuts the link to the operator. Such systems are also no longer prospective in our own region; they have been inducted into arsenals and recently used. These developments in the battlefield did not wait for the Geneva diplomatic community to settle first on a characterisation of LAWS or to spell out how the existing IHL applies to such systems. In 2013, Pakistan was among the first states to call for a legally binding prohibition on systems that decide on the use of force without human control and that do not allow a human user to understand, predict, and explain their decisions. As the technology evolved and was deployed on the battlefield, Pakistan also adapted its position to argue for a two-tier approach, with certain prohibitions in cases where IHL compliance could not be ensured, and restricting the use in all other cases. In its proposals submitted in 2023 and 2024, Pakistan laid out elements of a new legal instrument under this two-tier approach. It argued that any prohibition must cover development and not only use, since a weapon that is unlawful to use should not be lawful to build. Our position in support of a legal instrument found resonance and came to be shared by a majority of states, growing into a group of more than 100. An argument advanced by a handful of delegations 12 years ago has become the majority voice today. Technology on the battlefield has always outpaced the human ability to govern it. The record of arms control bears this out. Prohibitions have been agreed only where the weapon had not yet been fielded, as with blinding laser weapons, or where it offered no decisive advantage to the states that possessed it, as with biological weapons. It is difficult to find instances in which major military powers negotiated away the advantage they held on the battlefield. Restraint has been agreed for weapons that were marginal, obsolete, or not yet real. Autonomy in weapons is none of those things. For major powers, it has become the organising principle of the next generation of military doctrine and the largest defence-industrial investment of recent years. For other states, it has also become an instrument to offset asymmetries in different domains of warfare. It is unlikely that such states will accept meaningful constraints on these capabilities. While Pakistan will continue to argue for restraints, no state can be expected to rest its security on rules that do not yet exist, or on rules by which its adversaries have chosen not to be bound. Pakistan will keep a clear view of that reality and will need to take steps accordingly. The writer is a Pakistani diplomat, serving as counsellor in the Permanent Mission of Pakistan to the United Nations in Geneva and participating in the negotiations on the Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems.
articles.author: Husham Ahmed

articles.title: Beyond tariff cuts
articles.content: PAKISTAN cannot build a competitive industry by protecting it indefinitely. Nor can reducing protection, by itself, turn domestic manufacturers into exporters. Tariffs shape investment decisions, but competitiveness also depends on energy, technology, scale, supply chains, market access, and security. A credible industrial strategy must address them together. Unconditional protection raises prices, blunts incentives to innovate, and rewards selling to a captive home market. Consumers finance inefficiency, and capital chases protected returns rather than export opportunities. Where there is no credible prospect of competitiveness, protection merely postpones adjustment at public expense. TheNational Tariff Policy 2025-30, therefore, points broadly in the right direction. Fewer tariff slabs, cheaper imported inputs, and phased elimination of additional customs and regulatory duties can lower costs and reduce the bias against exports. But these are instruments of competitiveness, not substitutes for the conditions that make exports possible. The essential complement is a measurable programme to cut the costs the state imposes on production. If manufacturers face a timetable for lower protection, the government should face one for affordable, reliable energy, prompt tax refunds, simpler regulation, and efficient logistics. Otherwise, industry is asked to adjust while the state’s own contribution to uncompetitiveness goes unaddressed. This is not an argument for waiting until every domestic problem is solved; that would make protection permanent. It is a case for distinguishing activities with little prospect of competitiveness, those capable of achieving it, and a narrow set of strategic capabilities. The polyester chain shows the cost of failing to draw these distinctions. The textile industry association, APTMA, argues that protection on polyester staple fibre and its key input, purified terephthalic acid, raises costs for downstream textiles, while the country’s sole PTA plant, commissioned in 1998, lags newer plants in China and India. These claims by interested users warrant independent examination. The test is straightforward. Has prolonged support delivered globally competitive costs, technological upgrading, and lower energy use per tonne? Has it helped downstream producers compete in synthetic and blended textiles? Protection that preserves an inefficient input supplier while handicapping a much larger export opportunity defeats its own purpose. Energy illustrates the shared responsibility. High electricity tariffs and excessive electricity consumption are different problems: the government must fix the first; manufacturers must invest to reduce the second. Consumers and downstream exporters should not indefinitely finance either failure. Protection that preserves an inefficient input supplier while handicapping a much larger export opportunity defeats its own purpose. Yet an equally indiscriminate withdrawal of support could destroy capabilities with a viable future. Auto parts deserve assessment on this basis. Complaints about expensive vehicles and meagre exports obscure engineering skills within the supplier base. Toolmaking, casting, machining, moulding, process control, and quality assurance are not tied to one vehicle. Partnerships with foreign manufacturers can develop capabilities serving replacement markets, other engineering industries, and, where specifications permit, defence production. These capabilities justify scrutiny and selective development, not permanent protection for every assembler or component. The right unit of assessment is often the product or process, not the entire sector. Scale is crucial. Investment in moulds, testing or automated lines must be recovered over sufficient output; short runs make each unit expensive. Too many models fragment demand in a small market, while differing specifications prevent vendors from supplying the same part to several assemblers. Policy should encourage viable specialisation, common components where feasible, supplier consolidation, and access to replacement and export markets. A vendor serving several customers can reach volumes that no single low-volume model offers. Competition policy must accompany consolidation, so that scale raises productivity rather than market power. Upstream supply matters too. Reliable access to automotive-grade steel, engineering plastics and specialised chemicals affects quality, cost, lead times, and working capital. A competitive local supplier can shorten delivery and support joint development, but domestic steel or petrochemical production alone guarantees neither. Pakistan need not make every input before it can export. Where domestic production lacks scale or technology, predictable access to competitively priced imports is essential; forcing manufacturers to buy costly local inputs shifts protection upstream and erodes downstream competitiveness. The goal is an efficient supply chain combining viable domestic capabilities with dependable imports, not local-content targets. Market access is the next missing piece. Cutting Pakistan’s import tariffs does nothing to lower the duties its exporters face abroad. Preferential trade agreements can open larger markets, but their value depends on product coverage, rules of origin, and real commercial opportunities. They should be negotiated around what Pakistan can competitively supply and what investors could realistically produce. Buyers also weigh security. Export relationships depend on plant visits, technical assistance, audits, and dependable delivery. Insecurity, transport disruptions or barriers to foreign experts can cancel out a competitive price. Buyers pay for reliability, and investors need confidence that people, equipment and goods can travel safely. How, then, should protection be withdrawn? Activities with no credible route to competitiveness should have a clear exit timetable. Those with demonstrable potential should receive temporary support tied to investment, productivity, quality, energy efficiency, and a narrowing price gap with imports. Government should accept published obligations on costs and business conditions. An independent review should distinguish policy failures from outdated equipment, inadequate scale, or poor management. Verified government failures could justify limited adjustments to the tariff timetable, each with a firm expiry. Industry must not gain a permanent veto over reform. Strategic exceptions should remain narrow. Food security can justify agricultural resilience without self-sufficiency in every crop. Defence can justify selected domestic capabilities despite higher costs, subject to periodic review of their security value and expense. Lower tariffs on inputs remove one obstacle to exports. They cannot supply scale, modern technology, efficiency, market access, or security. Pakistan needs a reciprocal bargain: industry must earn support through performance, and the government must deliver conditions for competition. Neither should hand consumers an indefinite bill for its failures. The writeris a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and of the Pakistan Business Council.
articles.author: Ehsan Malik

articles.title: Spirit of cooperation
articles.content: FOR almost 80 years, Pakistanis have served under the UN flag, helping communities recover from conflict and rebuild peace. Pakistan has also provided refuge to millions fleeing instability. Pakistan has helped make international cooperation possible. Today, that spirit matters more than ever. Countries may disagree on politics, economics, and security, but share challenges none can resolve alone. Cooperation protects national interests. The UN secretary-general’s message was clear during his recent visit to Pakistan: no country can tackle interconnected challenges alone. Conflict disrupts trade and raises food and energy costs; climate change threatens water, agriculture and livelihoods; pandemics and artificial intelligence bring cross-border risks and opportunities. For Pakistan, these connections are not theoretical. The devastating floods of 2022 caused an estimated $30 billion in damage and economic losses, with women and children among those facing the most lasting consequences. The floods of 2025 brought another reminder of the human and economic costs of climate-related disasters. Building resilience requires strong national leadership, effective domestic resource allocation, and better development of vulnerable communities, but also international solidarity, climate finance, and partnerships. Pakistan’s recent diplomacy offers another illustration. The secretary-general praised Pakistan’s role in facilitating dialogue between the United States and Iran. Such efforts cannot guarantee peace, but they show why diplomacy matters: even when interests diverge sharply, keeping channels open can create possibilities that confrontation alone cannot. Pakistan’s contribution to UN peacekeeping and its long-standing role in hosting refugees reflect the same understanding. A more peaceful region, functioning international institutions, and respect for international law matter directly to Pakistan’s security and prosperity. What are countries choosing to do about a divided world? The stakes are also domestic. Pakistan’s population of around 255 million includes a vast young generation. Realising its potential depends on access to quality education, relevant skills, and decent work. Turning demographic scale into an economic dividend requires sustained national investment and international partnership. Women and girls, people with disabilities, and other marginalised groups must be able to shape and share in that opportunity; otherwise, inequality will hold back progress. Defending multilateralism does not mean defending every aspect of today’s institutions. Many people question whether international cooperation can deliver solutions to the problems they face in daily life. Those concerns deserve to be taken seriously. The answer is not less multilateralism, but better multilateralism: more effective, more representative and better equipped to deliver. The secretary-general’s UN80 initiative is part of that effort. But reform is a shared responsibility: Member states should provide the political leadership and resources needed to make cooperation work, while holding the UN accountable for delivering on its mandates. The UN Charter’s principles remain essential: sovereign equality, peaceful settlement of disputes, international law, and human rights. They are not always upheld consistently. That is a reason to demand greater accountability, not discard them. When rules apply selectively, trust erodes and every country is more exposed. Weaker cooperation has real consequences: lives lost to conflict and disaster, livelihoods destroyed, girls pushed out of school and opportunities denied to young people. The UN provides a place to negotiate, coordinate action, and support people facing crises. It cannot resolve every conflict, but can help keep dialogue open and turn commitments into results. Pakistan’s commitment to the multilateral system was also recognised when President Asif Ali Zardari conferred the Nishan-i-Imtiaz on Secretary-General Guterres on Oct 6 — the first time Pakistan has bestowed the honour on a serving UN secretary-general. It recognised his service and the long-standing Pakistan-UN partnership. On United Nations Day, the question is not whether the world is divided. It plainly is. The question is what countries choose to do about it. In a world where we cannot control every change taking place around us and so many challenges cross borders, we can choose whether to meet the challenge through confrontation or cooperation; division or dialogue; unilateralism or solidarity. For Pakistan, as for every country, cooperation, dialogue and solidarity are not concessions of sovereignty. They are investments in a more stable, sustainable and prosperous future. The writer is United Nations resident coordinator (ad interim) in Pakistan.
articles.author: Pernille Ironside

articles.title: AIPAC’s shift
articles.content: ON Wednesday, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) made an unusualannouncement. The organisation would no longer endorse or make direct contributions to candidates running in US elections. This marks the end of a practice that AIPAC began in 2021 (its lobbying started in the ‘50s). This does not mean that the Israel lobby will stop trying to influence US elections. AIPAC will continue mobilising individual donors. However, the announcement is an acknowledgement of the growing difficulties associated with overt affiliation with the lobby and the pro-Israel agenda. The genocide in Gazaand thewar in Iranhave created a situation where many Americans are questioning their country’s support for Israel and the resources devoted to it. Democratic candidates have challenged US involvement in the Middle East and the $3.8 billion in annual assistance Washington provides Israel. No campaign has illustrated this with greater clarity than that of Dr Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the US Senate seat in Michigan. In the Democratic primary, AIPAC spent $30 million backing El-Sayed’s opponent, Haley Stevens. Other political action committees also spent heavily on her campaign. In contrast, El-Sayed spent only $3.2m, most of it raised from individual donors. Despite all this, El-Sayed won. One reason was his willingness to confront Stevens over AIPAC’s involvement in the race and to question why US taxpayer money should go to another country. What El-Sayed was able to do is connect two different realities of the American political context. First, he tapped into the American fatigue with interminable wars in the Middle East. Again, and again, he argued that the US had “no business” becoming embroiled in further conflicts, while infrastructure and institutions at home were decaying. His criticism of Donald Trump’s escapades in Iran became part of this argument. Second, El-Sayed connected the affordability crisis facing Americans to questions about government spending and the country’s relationship with Israel. Americans struggling to afford healthcare and basic groceries are naturally questioning how public money is spent abroad. War-weary Americans can see through Israeli machinations. El-Sayed is not campaigning on Israel alone. Affordability and healthcare are central issues for him, and he supports a government-funded Medicare For All option that would make healthcare accessible to millions of people. His own background in public health makes him a persuasive speaker on these issues. AIPAC’s affiliated Super PAC has now directed spending against El-Sayed in his contest with Republican Mike Rogers. This is a departure from AIPAC’s usual support for Democratic candidates in Michigan. American Zionists and the well-heeled donors behind AIPAC may see the Michigan contest not simply as an electoral battle in a US state but also as an indicator of how anti-Israel sentiment is becoming increasingly pervasive among the Democratic electorate. The announcement that there will be no more overt endorsements reflects the liability that public association with AIPAC can create for some candidates. It is a sea change in the character of Democratic politics in the US. There are global implications in this shift. If El-Sayed wins — and one hopes he does despite the millions that AIPAC is now pouring into his opponent’s coffers — it will mean that other Democratic lawmakers in the House and Senate will have to think twice about voting to send billions of dollars to Israel. In the past, Democratic politicians have voted en masse for just these sorts of measures. Israel is very proud of its genocidal actions in Gaza. It is also quite smug about having persuaded Trump to attack Iran. It sees both of these actions and its continuing excesses in Gaza and the West Bank as victories. This, however, is an illusion. The reality is that in the process of achieving the former, Israelis forgot that ordinary, war-weary Americans can see through its machinations. This is important not because Israel cares what Americans think but because Israel is entirely dependent on the US, receiving almost 70 per cent of its military equipment from them. As the election of Zohran Mamdani in New York City and the hopeful rise of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan show, Americans are signalling just how fed up they are with Israel’s intrusions in their own government and its attempts to create dual loyalties in their political leadership. As American leaders stop signing blank cheques for Israel as in the past five decades, Israel is likely to face enormous struggles. Already an isolated nation, increasingly detested by the world for the carnage of innocents, its future is not that of a victorious nation but of a widely reviled one. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: Breaking the cycle
articles.content: THE World Bank’s latest Pakistan Development Update sets out what faster reforms could deliver for the economy. If policies and institutions matched those of an average middle-income country, it estimates, annual growthcould reach 6.2-6.9pc, enough to reach Vietnam’s current income level, and incomes would triple by 2050. The distance from here is long. Real GDP growth rose to 3.65pc in FY26 and the primary surplus reached 2.9pc of GDP. But per capita income is currently growing at only about 1.6pc, which means the economy has been put in better financial order without making most people better off. The country’s return to macroeconomic stability is widely appreciated by international lenders and credit agencies. However, it is not the same thing as a solid foundation for rapid growth. Much of this stability has come from holding the economy down. High interest rates, fiscal tightening, and costly energy have dampened demand and squeezed imports, easing pressure on the external account. Workers’ remittances have helped the current account and rebuilt reserves, and continued external borrowing has bought time. But none of this builds capacity. Borrowing defers the bill, remittances bring in dollars without adding to domestic output, and compressed imports can fix the external balance while leaving exports no more competitive. The stability that results depends on inflows continuing and on the government keeping up its restraint. That is why any real push for growth can be risky. It would mean more imported machinery, fuel, industrial inputs, and consumer goods. If exports and productivity do not keep pace, the current account slips, reserves fall, and policymakers enforce tightening again. We have been through this cycle many times. Breaking it means changing what the economy produces and sells, not just how fast it is allowed to grow. The obstacles are well known: unreliable and costly energy, a narrow tax base, cumbersome regulation, weak competition, and a poorly skilled workforce. Policy keeps changing, which deters long-term investment. Tax reform must bring undertaxed sectors into the net, instead of increasing the burden on those already compliant. Energy reform has to cut system costs rather than shift them between consumers and the budget. And exports need a policy that works beyond incentives. Macroeconomic stability cannot carry the economy much further without better productivity. The World Bank’s numbers are best read as a reform target. Reaching Vietnam’s income level will take sustained spending on education, health, infrastructure, and technology, and institutions that can be trusted. It will also take growth that creates more than just better headline figures. If the government does not use the present breathing space to raise productivity, boost exports, and complete lasting energy and tax reforms, the next growth push could bring back the crisis Pakistan has just come out of.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Gaza starvation
articles.content: ON account of funding cuts and Israeli cruelty, the threat of famine once again looms over the occupied Gaza Strip. The World Food Programme says it is reducing food assistance to Palestinians in the Strip due to funding shortages. The move will affect half a million people, many in dire need of food aid to survive. Prices of what little food is available have started climbing in the devastated Strip, while many bakeries have been shuttered. Also impacting the availability of food is Israel’s stranglehold on what enters Gaza. Under last year’s ceasefire deal, Israel had pledged to let in 600 aid trucks daily; only a fraction of that number actually arrives. It should be remembered that a famine had been declared in Gaza last year. The UN says that around two-thirds of Gaza’s people continue to face “acute food insecurity”. While Israel does all it can to stop aid from coming into the occupied territory, the Zionist state — similar to the barbarians of antiquity — has also destroyed Gaza’s food sources. The FAO says only 3pc of Gaza’s cropland “remains accessible and undamaged”, while the Strip’s fishing industry has also been destroyed. Many in the international community remained silent as Gaza endured a genocide and manmade famine. It would be beyond criminal if its people are forced to live through another, entirely preventable famine. If there are financial constraints, then the world community — including those states that have armed and funded Israel — should open its coffers to fill the gaps in food aid. The US — both the Biden and Trump administrations — poured billions of dollars into Israel. It is now America’s moral duty to ensure food reaches Gaza. Moreover, many members of the Muslim world with deep pockets — who only paid lip service to Gaza — must step in and contribute to alleviating the region’s hunger. But most of all, Israel must be held to account for precipitating famine, destroying Gaza’s food sources, and starving the Palestinian people — a war crime under international law, even though the Zionist state is no stranger to committing such atrocious deeds. All obstacles standing in the way of aid reaching Gaza must be immediately lifted, and the Strip’s residents should get the nutrition, healthcare, and sanitation services they require.
